The demand for large, labeled datasets has fueled the widespread adoption of crowdsourcing platforms like Amazon’s Mechanical Turk (AMT) for various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. These platforms offer a cost-effective and scalable solution for obtaining annotations – crucial for training supervised machine learning models and evaluating system performance. However, a critical challenge arises from the inherent variability in annotator quality. Unlike expert annotators, individuals participating in crowdsourcing often lack specific domain expertise and may be motivated by financial incentives rather than accuracy, leading to the submission of intentionally incorrect or carelessly produced labels – often referred to as “spam” or “low-quality” contributions. Identifying and filtering out these unreliable annotations is essential to prevent detrimental impacts on model training and evaluation. While manual inspection remains a gold standard, it is demonstrably expensive, time-consuming, and impractical for datasets of substantial size. Existing approaches to quality control frequently rely on techniques like redundancy (collecting multiple annotations per instance and aggregating them), gold questions (embedding pre-validated instances to assess annotator reliability), or reputation systems built around historical performance. These methods, while effective to a degree, often come with limitations. Redundancy significantly increases annotation costs. Gold questions can be vulnerable to collusion and may not generalize well across different task types. Reputation systems can be slow to accurately reflect annotator performance, particularly for new contributors. This paper introduces MACE (Multi-Annotator Competence Estimation), a novel unsupervised approach to simultaneously estimate annotator trustworthiness and predict correct labels, directly addressing the shortcomings of existing quality control methodologies. Unlike prior work often relying on explicitly modeling noise distributions or incorporating complex prior knowledge, MACE leverages an item-response modeling (IRM) framework. IRM provides a probabilistic model for relating annotator responses to underlying item (in our case, data instance) characteristics, allowing us to infer both annotator competence and latent true labels without requiring any pre-labeled data. A key advantage of our formulation is its ability to learn these parameters *jointly*; an annotator’s deemed competence influences the weight given to their responses when inferring the underlying true labels, and vice-versa. We demonstrate that MACE achieves performance competitive with, and in some cases exceeding, more sophisticated state-of-the-art quality estimation systems, including those employing actively learned or semi-supervised techniques. Notably, MACE proves robust even under adversarial conditions, where a significant fraction of annotators intentionally submit incorrect responses. We further show that incorporating a prior distribution on model parameters through Variational Bayes inference enhances the accuracy of trustworthiness estimation. Moreover, we explore strategies for maximizing performance by focusing on instances where the model exhibits high confidence and leveraging a small set of expertly annotated control instances – a practical setting reflecting limited expert resources. MACE is publicly available to facilitate wider adoption and further research in this critical area of crowdsourced data quality. Through these contributions, we aim to provide a practical and effective solution for “learning whom to trust” within large-scale annotation tasks, ultimately improving the quality and reliability of datasets used to drive progress in NLP.

## Introduction The ability to engage in coherent, informative, and engaging dialogue has long been a central goal of Natural Language Processing. Recent advancements in neural network architectures, particularly sequence-to-sequence models and transformers, have yielded significant progress in dialog generation. However, current systems often struggle with maintaining long-term coherence, providing contextually relevant responses, and demonstrating genuine reasoning capabilities – particularly in multi-turn conversations. A common limitation stems from treating each turn in a dialogue as an isolated event, failing to effectively leverage the accumulated conversational history to inform response generation. While techniques like hierarchical recurrent neural networks and attention mechanisms have partially addressed this issue, they often fall short of truly capturing the dynamic and evolving context of a conversation. A burgeoning area of research in natural language understanding, multi-turn reasoning, offers a potential pathway to overcome these limitations. Initially developed for tasks like question answering over long documents, multi-turn reasoning techniques focus on iterative reading and reasoning over information sources. These methods progressively refine understanding by performing multiple passes of attention over the source material, accumulating evidence and drawing inferences. We hypothesize that adapting this reasoning paradigm to dialogue generation could significantly enhance the quality and coherence of generated responses. In this work, we propose a novel dialog generation framework that explicitly incorporates multi-turn reasoning principles. We reconceptualize a conversation session as a “document” and the current user query as a “question,” allowing us to leverage the powerful mechanisms of multi-turn reading comprehension. Unlike previous approaches that often compress the entire dialogue history into a single contextual vector, our method represents the conversation as a structured collection of memories, enabling the model to iteratively attend to relevant pieces of information. A key contribution of our work lies in recognizing that conversations are inherently multi-party interactions. The conversational context is shaped not only by the user's statements but also by the system's responses and the interplay between differing perspectives. To address this, we dissect the shared memory space into distinct groups – a query memory, a response memory, and a unified memory – each capturing different facets of the conversational dynamics. This separation allows the model to explicitly differentiate between the originating queries, the system’s previous responses, and the evolving shared understanding built throughout the conversation. By sequentially accessing and reasoning over these memories, our model can better extend and contextualize the current query, leading to the step-by-step generation of more pertinent and satisfying responses. We evaluate our approach on a challenging Japanese dialog dataset consisting of 10-sentence (5-round) conversations. Our empirical results demonstrate that our multi-turn reasoning framework significantly outperforms strong baseline models, including both single-turn generation systems and non-reasoning multi-turn models, in terms of both response diversity and overall acceptability. This work provides a strong indication that incorporating multi-turn reasoning is crucial for building truly intelligent and engaging dialogue agents. <!-- I have kept the output only as the intro section.-->

The ability to represent and reason about meaning is central to natural language processing. For decades, this has been approached through symbolic methods, relying on hand-crafted lexicons and explicit compositional rules. However, the limitations of such approaches—their brittleness, difficulty in scaling to large vocabularies, and inability to capture nuanced semantic variation—have spurred a growing interest in distributional semantics (DS). DS posits that the meaning of a word is encoded in its usage, specifically in the contexts in which it appears. Over the last two decades, this principle has been successfully leveraged to develop algorithms that capture surprisingly robust semantic representations of single words by analyzing their distributions in large text corpora and representing them as vectors in a high-dimensional space. However, representing the meaning of multi-word expressions – phrases, sentences, or even entire documents – presents a significant challenge. While representing individual words via distributional methods is now well-established, *composing* these individual representations to form a coherent representation of a larger unit remains a fundamentally difficult problem. Simply summing or averaging word vectors, while computationally efficient, often fails to capture the complex interactions between words that determine the overall meaning. The semantic relationship between “red” and “book” is not simply the sum of the individual meanings of “red” and “book”; it depends on how these words combine to define a specific type of book. Existing approaches to compositional distributional semantics can broadly be categorized, with varying degrees of success. Some methods rely on linear algebra, attempting to model composition using operations like addition, multiplication, or tensor products. Others introduce more complex, learnable parameters to mediate the compositional process, often leveraging neural networks. Still others build on earlier linguistic theories, such as lexical functions, which attempt to capture the semantic roles words play in combination. Baroni and Zamparelli (2010) introduced a powerful method centering on lexical functions, demonstrating the importance of explicitly modeling how words modify each other’s meanings during composition, specifically focusing on adjective-noun pairings. Despite the proliferation of methods, a comprehensive understanding of their relative strengths and weaknesses is lacking, particularly with respect to different types of compositional relationships. Many evaluations are performed on limited datasets or focus on a single type of composition (e.g., adjective-noun). Furthermore, the theoretical underpinnings of successful composition functions are still debated. In this work, we address these gaps with a two-fold contribution. First, we present a large-scale evaluation of several prominent compositional distributional semantic models, focusing specifically on both adjective-noun and noun-noun composition. Critically, this evaluation utilizes a newly developed dataset designed to rigorously assess compositional performance. Second, we introduce a novel compositional method that generalizes the approach pioneered by Baroni and Zamparelli (2010). Our generalization builds on the core intuition of lexical functions but extends it to a broader range of compositional scenarios, and is trainable end-to-end. We demonstrate, through extensive experimentation on our new dataset, that our method achieves competitive results compared to state-of-the-art compositional models, suggesting a promising direction for future research in distributional semantics.

Knowledge bases (KBs) represent structured knowledge as entities and relations, offering a powerful foundation for a wide range of natural language processing applications. A critical task within this realm is knowledge base completion (KBC), aiming to infer missing facts – triples of (head entity, relation, tail entity) – that are likely to be true but not explicitly stated in the KB. Recent years have witnessed a surge in embedding-based KBC models, which learn low-dimensional vector representations of entities and relations, enabling the prediction of plausible missing links. A particularly effective strategy for enriching these embeddings is to leverage *relation paths* – sequences of relations connecting two entities within the KB. The intuition is that entities related by meaningful paths are more likely to be connected by implicit facts. For instance, if we observe that ‘Barack Obama’ *born_in* ‘Honolulu’ and ‘Honolulu’ *is_a* ‘City’, the path `born_in -> is_a` strengthens the likelihood of a relationship between ‘Barack Obama’ and the broader concept of ‘City’. However, the straightforward application of relation paths faces significant scalability challenges. The number of possible paths between two entities grows exponentially with the path length, rendering exhaustive enumeration infeasible for real-world KBs. Consequently, most existing approaches rely on sampling a limited subset of paths, which inevitably leads to a loss of crucial relational information. This is further complicated when considering the integration of textual knowledge. More and more research has begun to focus on *jointly* modeling KBs and text, recognizing that natural language often provides direct evidence for facts stored in KBs. When dealing with text, the need for comprehensive path information becomes even more pressing. A sentence like "Obama, born in Honolulu, is a former president" directly links Obama to Honolulu through the ‘born_in’ relation, and effectively provides a justification for that relationship within the KB. Effectively capturing these interconnections requires not just acknowledging the existence of the path but accurately representing its *compositionality* – how the individual relations and intermediate entities contribute to the overall meaning and predictive power. Prior work often struggles to represent the full compositional impact, treating paths as monolithic units or relying on simplified approximations. In this paper, we address the limitations of existing approaches by introducing a novel method for the compositional learning of embeddings for relation paths. We present the first exact dynamic programming algorithm that enables the efficient incorporation of *all* relation paths of a bounded length, while simultaneously modeling both relation types and intermediate nodes in the compositional path representations. This dynamic programming approach dramatically reduces the computational burden compared to naive exhaustive enumeration, offering a significant improvement in efficiency. We provide a thorough theoretical analysis confirming these gains, demonstrating the algorithm's scalability. Furthermore, we demonstrate empirically, on two benchmark datasets, that our approach addresses crucial representational limitations inherent in previous methods and leads to substantial improvements in KB completion accuracy, particularly in scenarios where textual context is leveraged alongside KB information. Our work paves the way for more expressive and accurate joint KB and text embedding models, ultimately enhancing our ability to reason over complex relational structures.

Discourse relations, the semantic connections between segments of text, are fundamental to human comprehension. Recognizing these relations—whether explicit (marked by discourse connectives like “because” or “however”) or implicit (requiring inferencing)—is crucial for tasks ranging from text summarization and machine translation to question answering and reading comprehension. While explicit discourse relation detection has seen significant progress, identifying *implicit* relations remains a substantial challenge in Natural Language Processing. These relations, devoid of overt linguistic cues, rely on subtle semantic and pragmatic cues, demanding a deeper understanding of the context and the interplay between arguments. Traditional approaches to implicit discourse relation recognition have largely relied on feature engineering, employing hand-crafted features based on lexical overlap, syntactic structure, and semantic similarity. More recently, neural network models have gained prominence, leveraging sequence encoding with recurrent neural networks (RNNs) or transformers to capture contextual information. However, a common limitation of these models is their tendency to process the input text – typically a sentence pair constituting the arguments – in a single pass. This single-pass approach, while computationally efficient, often overlooks the nuanced process humans employ when interpreting text. We posit that effective comprehension, particularly when faced with implicit cues, frequently involves *repeated reading*—a dynamic process where attention is iteratively refined, focusing on different aspects of the text with each pass. A reader doesn’t grasp a discourse relation immediately; rather, they revisit the arguments, weighting different words and phrases based on their evolving hypothesis about the connection. Initial reads might focus on broad contextual clues, while subsequent reads zero in on specific indicators related to the potential relation. This iterative refinement allows for a more nuanced and flexible understanding that adjusts as new information is considered. Inspired by this cognitive process, we introduce Neural Networks with Multi-Level Attention (NNMA), a novel architecture designed to mimic repeated reading for implicit discourse relation recognition. NNMA incorporates external memories alongside attention mechanisms. The external memory allows the model to store and revisit representations of the arguments at different levels of abstraction. The multi-level attention mechanism then dynamically focuses on relevant information within these representations during each ‘reading’ or attention step. This tiered approach differs significantly from standard attention models that typically operate on a single level of representation. Crucially, the model doesn't simply *attend* to the input; it *revisits* it, refining its attention weights and focusing on increasingly refined features that support the identification of the underlying discourse relation. We evaluate NNMA on the widely used Penn Discourse Treebank (PDTB) dataset, demonstrating that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance. Furthermore, visualization of the attention weights reveals the progressive nature of the model’s analysis, illustrating how it sequentially attends to different aspects of the arguments, culminating in the identification of key words indicative of the discourse relation. This provides compelling evidence that NNMA effectively captures the essence of repeated reading and leverages it for improved implicit discourse relation recognition. This paper details the architecture of NNMA, our experimental setup, results, and analysis, contributing a new perspective on how to approach this challenging NLP problem.

The explosive growth of social media platforms has created a vast repository of user-generated text, offering unprecedented opportunities for social and linguistic analysis. However, this data presents significant challenges for Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks. Unlike formal writing, social media text is characterized by its informality, including widespread use of slang, misspellings, abbreviations, and grammatical errors. This non-standard language significantly hinders the performance of standard NLP tools, which are typically trained on clean, well-formed text. Consequently, a crucial first step in processing social media text is *text normalization* – the process of transforming non-standard words and phrases into their standard, canonical forms. Text normalization directly impacts a wide range of downstream NLP applications, including sentiment analysis, topic modeling, information retrieval, and machine translation. For instance, accurately identifying the sentiment expressed in a tweet requires correctly interpreting variations like “lol,” “lmao,” and “haha” as expressions of amusement. Similarly, effective topic modeling relies on consolidating different spellings of the same word (e.g., “nite” and “night”) to accurately represent the underlying thematic content. Early approaches to text normalization relied heavily on manually curated dictionaries mapping non-standard forms to their standardized equivalents. However, creating and maintaining such dictionaries is a laborious, expensive, and ultimately limited endeavor, unable to keep pace with the ever-evolving landscape of online language. More recent work has focused on leveraging statistical methods and machine learning techniques to address this challenge. Many of these methods, while improving upon dictionary-based approaches, still predominantly focus on lexical similarity – identifying normalization candidates based on string edit distance or phonetic matching. While these techniques are valuable, they often fall short of capturing the nuanced relationship between words and their context, leading to incorrect or suboptimal normalizations. The core limitation of many existing techniques lies in their neglect of the rich contextual and grammatical information inherent in social media text. Words are rarely used in isolation; their meaning and correct form are often determined by their surrounding linguistic environment. To address this, we propose a novel, unsupervised text normalization approach that explicitly models contextual and grammatical dependencies through the construction and utilization of a word association graph. This graph, built from a large corpus of unlabeled social media data, encapsulates relationships between words based on their co-occurrence patterns and part-of-speech (POS) tags. Our approach differs fundamentally from those reliant on generating comprehensive normalization dictionaries. Instead of searching for the *closest* match based solely on surface similarity, we leverage the graph to *infer* the most likely standard form of a non-standard word given its contextual surroundings. This permits the system to deal effectively with previously unseen variations, and to disambiguate ambiguous forms with greater accuracy. We integrate this contextual information with established lexical similarity measures – longest common subsequence ratio, edit distance, and double metaphone – offering a robust and complementary feature set. Through extensive experimentation on standard text normalization datasets, we demonstrate that our graph-based approach achieves state-of-the-art F-score performance. Furthermore, we show that the system can be readily tuned to prioritize precision without substantial loss in recall, making it a versatile tool for diverse applications. Our contributions, therefore, lie in the development of a novel contextualized normalization framework, a graph-based representation capable of encoding valuable linguistic information, and the empirical demonstration of its superior performance.

Bilingual dictionary induction (BDI) – the task of automatically discovering translation equivalences between words in two languages – remains a cornerstone of machine translation, cross-lingual information retrieval, and countless other natural language processing applications. Despite decades of research, achieving high-accuracy BDI, particularly for low-resource language pairs, continues to pose a significant challenge. Traditional approaches, reliant on parallel corpora or comparable corpora, often falter when such resources are scarce or non-existent. Recently, a promising paradigm has emerged leveraging zero-shot learning to map word vector spaces across languages, sidestepping the direct need for parallel data. These zero-shot methods typically learn a mapping function – often linear – that projects word embeddings from a source language into the vector space of a target language, enabling the identification of nearest neighbors as potential translations. However, despite their conceptual elegance and avoidance of parallel data dependency, the performance of these methods has consistently lagged behind approaches that benefit from even modest amounts of parallel data, particularly when addressing languages with limited resources. A key bottleneck lies in the difficulty of learning robust and accurate mapping functions with limited cross-lingual signal. Effective alignment requires capturing nuanced semantic relationships that are often difficult to discern with sparse data. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to BDI that directly tackles this challenge by leveraging the principle of knowledge distillation. Our central hypothesis is that the knowledge encoded in translation paths derived from resource-rich language pairs can be effectively transferred to improve the performance of translation paths involving low-resource languages. We frame this as a teacher-student learning scenario: we exploit readily available, high-quality translation paths—for instance, English-Spanish, English-French—as ‘teachers,’ and low-resource paths – such as Nepali-English or Khmer-English – as ‘students.’ The core of our contribution lies in a specifically designed knowledge distillation training objective that encourages the student (low-resource) translation paths to mimic the behavior of the teacher (high-resource) paths. This differs from prior work which often focuses on directly aligning embeddings or using pre-trained multilingual models. Our approach allows for the *seamless addition* of any number of teacher translation paths, offering adaptability and scalability to diverse language combinations. Critically, the distillation process isn’t about forcing exact embedding alignment, but about transferring the *relational* knowledge learned by the teacher regarding word similarities and differences within the context of translation. Furthermore, recognizing the foundational role of high-quality word embeddings, we enhance the vector representations of both source and target languages by incorporating linguistic information. This augmentation aims to provide a more semantically informed basis for the knowledge distillation process. We achieve this by integrating character-level information and morphological features, enhancing the embeddings with information often absent in standard word embedding training procedures. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through extensive experiments across several low-resource language pairs. Our results indicate substantial performance gains – up to 17% absolute accuracy improvement – attributed to the distilled knowledge from resource-rich languages. This work represents a significant step toward more effective and scalable bilingual dictionary induction, particularly for the vast majority of language pairs lacking substantial parallel resources.

## Introduction The pursuit of truly engaging and human-like dialogue systems has been a central challenge in Natural Language Processing for decades. Early systems relied heavily on handcrafted rules and templates, offering limited flexibility and often producing stilted, predictable responses. More recently, sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models, powered by recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and, increasingly, transformers, have demonstrated remarkable progress in generating coherent and contextually relevant dialogue. However, despite these advances, current neural dialogue models often suffer from issues such as generic responses (e.g., “I don’t know,” “That’s interesting”), a lack of consistency, and a general inability to exhibit the nuance and creativity characteristic of human conversation. Fundamentally, a key difficulty lies in defining a robust and reliable reward signal for training these models. Traditional approaches often rely on metrics like BLEU, ROUGE, or perplexity, which evaluate the *similarity* between generated responses and a set of reference responses. However, these metrics are known to correlate poorly with human judgments of dialogue quality. A high score on BLEU does not necessarily equate to a helpful, engaging, or insightful response; a model can achieve a decent BLEU score by simply mimicking the most frequent patterns in the training data, resulting in bland and unoriginal outputs. Moreover, the existence of multiple valid responses to a given prompt renders the concept of a single “correct” reference response problematic for supervised learning. Inspired by the seminal Turing Test, we propose a novel approach to neural dialogue generation based on adversarial learning. The Turing Test, in its essence, assesses a machine’s ability to exhibit intelligent behavior equivalent to, or indistinguishable from, that of a human. We translate this core idea into a training paradigm where a dialogue generation model is pitted against an adversarial *discriminator* whose task is to distinguish between machine-generated and human-generated dialogue utterances. The generator aims to produce responses that “fool” the discriminator, effectively learning to mimic the characteristics of human conversation. We formulate this interaction as a reinforcement learning (RL) problem. The generative model acts as the “agent,” attempting to maximize a reward signal provided by the discriminator. Successful deception – generating a response that the discriminator identifies as human-authored – yields a positive reward, while detection leads to a negative reward. This adversarial training process encourages the generator to move beyond simply matching surface-level similarities with training data and to learn deeper patterns of human language use, ultimately fostering the generation of more natural and engaging dialogue. Beyond the training methodology, we also introduce a new evaluation metric rooted in adversarial principles. Rather than relying on traditional metrics, our evaluation assesses a model’s ability to consistently fool a separate, pre-trained adversarial discriminator. This provides a more direct and intuitive measure of dialogue quality, reflecting the system’s capacity to convincingly simulate human conversation. We carefully address potential pitfalls inherent in adversarial evaluation, such as discriminator overfitting and sensitivity to subtle linguistic cues. Through a comprehensive set of experiments, we demonstrate that our adversarially-trained model consistently outperforms strong baselines on both automatic metrics and, crucially, our proposed adversarial evaluation. This work represents a significant step towards building dialogue systems that are not merely fluent, but truly capable of engaging in believable and satisfying conversations with humans.

Query spelling correction is a crucial component of modern information retrieval systems. Despite advancements in automatic speech recognition and text input methods, user queries frequently contain spelling errors – a consequence of typing speed, phonetic similarity between words, and simple carelessness. These errors hinder search effectiveness, leading to zero-result pages and frustrated users. Accurately correcting these queries is therefore paramount to delivering a positive search experience and maximizing information access. Early approaches to query spelling correction largely relied on model-based techniques, particularly noisy channel models (NCMs). NCMs elegantly frame the problem as decoding a noisy observation (the misspelled query) into the most probable original query, leveraging language models and edit distance calculations to estimate the probabilities of error generation and word likelihood. While effective as a first pass, NCMs often struggle with complex errors, context-dependent nuances, and a lack of robustness to out-of-vocabulary words. Moreover, they typically treat the correction problem as independent word errors, ignoring valuable structural information within the query. Recent research has shifted towards a two-stage paradigm, recognizing the limitations of purely generative models. This approach first employs an NCM or similar retrieval mechanism to generate a candidate set of potential corrections. This candidate generation step, while imperfect in its recall, serves to significantly reduce the search space. The second stage then utilizes a discriminative model – typically a ranking function – to re-rank these candidates and select the most appropriate correction. This discriminative refinement allows the system to learn directly from features that differentiate correct corrections from incorrect ones, leveraging labeled training data to optimize for search effectiveness metrics. However, this two-stage approach faces a critical bottleneck: the performance of the discriminative ranker is fundamentally limited by the quality of the candidate set generated by the first stage. A noisy channel model with low recall inevitably misses potentially valid corrections, and the ranker, no matter how sophisticated, cannot recover options that were never presented to it. Consequently, the discriminative ranker is often forced to choose the “least bad” option from a suboptimal selection, leading to suboptimal overall correction accuracy. Previous discriminative models, frequently employing point-wise or pair-wise learning-to-rank methods, have largely treated each candidate independently, effectively ignoring the relationships *between* candidates within a given query. This overlooks crucial structural information. For instance, recognizing that two candidates differ by only a single character edit might indicate a stronger likelihood of a shared underlying error. In this paper, we present a novel discriminative model for query spelling correction that directly addresses these limitations. We propose a Latent Structural Support Vector Machine (SVM) framework that moves beyond independent candidate evaluation, explicitly modeling the latent structure inherent in the candidate set. This allows the model to learn relationships between candidate corrections and incorporate that structural information into the ranking process. By jointly considering the entire set of candidates for a given query, our model can leverage subtle cues that would be lost in a purely independent evaluation, leading to improved correction performance, particularly in scenarios where the initial candidate generation stage exhibits low recall. We demonstrate through extensive experimentation on benchmark datasets that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art discriminative query spelling correction models.

Tree-to-tree transduction forms a cornerstone of many natural language processing applications, from machine translation and parsing to semantic parsing and question answering. These models map input trees (often representing syntactic structure) to output trees (representing, for example, logical forms or target language structures). Historically, statistical tree transducers have proven highly effective, often relying on probabilistic context-free grammars (PCFGs) extended to operate on tree structures, or neural network architectures capable of learning complex mappings. A critical step in building such systems, however, is *rule extraction* – the process of inducing the transduction rules from parallel tree/string (or tree/tree) data. Current state-of-the-art approaches frequently depend on leveraging word alignments, particularly in settings where the target output is string-based. These alignments are then used to heuristically guide the extraction of rules that connect source and target structures. While effective in many scenarios, this reliance on word alignments introduces a significant vulnerability: performance degrades substantially when the available training corpus is relatively small compared to the vocabulary size or the inherent complexity of the transduction task. Sparse data leads to unreliable alignments, hindering the accurate identification of correspondences between source and target elements, and ultimately diminishing the quality of the extracted rules. Consider, for example, the task of mapping natural language questions to formal queries over a knowledge base (KB). Such systems require accurately translating the syntactic structure of the question into the logical form needed to access relevant information within the KB. In these scenarios, the vocabulary of possible questions and KB entities can be extremely large, while the number of available question-query pairs may be limited. Traditional alignment-based rule extraction struggles because it’s difficult to establish reliable word-to-KB-element mappings with limited training data. This paper addresses this challenge by proposing a novel rule extraction algorithm for tree-to-tree transducers that *minimizes cost* over tree fragments rather than relying on word alignments. Our approach defines cost functions that evaluate the “goodness” of potential rule components based on structural features and distributional information captured within the training data. The rule extraction process is then framed as a cost minimization problem, seeking to identify the set of rules that collectively yield the lowest overall cost across the training set. Crucially, our method incorporates a dynamic back-off mechanism. When encountering a previously unseen left-hand side (LHS) during rule application, the system intelligently generates right-hand sides (RHS) “on-the-fly” by leveraging lower-cost alternatives. This allows the transducer to gracefully handle novel input structures and expand its coverage without being limited by the rules explicitly observed during training. This capability contrasts sharply with traditional static rule sets, which often suffer from poor generalization performance on unseen data. We evaluate the effectiveness of our approach on a question answering (QA) task over a large knowledge base. The results demonstrate not only reasonable syntactic accuracy but, more importantly, the ability to overcome the inherent limitations of sparse training data and achieve effective rule coverage. We show that the cost minimization framework, combined with the dynamic back-off strategy, enables the induction of robust tree transducers capable of generalizing to unseen queries and providing accurate KB access.

The ability to understand and reason about everyday events is a hallmark of human intelligence, yet remains a significant challenge for natural language processing (NLP) systems. At the core of this challenge lies the representation and acquisition of *commonsense knowledge* – the vast, largely implicit understanding of the world that humans effortlessly employ to interpret language and navigate daily life. This is particularly acute when grappling with the nuanced relationships between events; understanding *why* things happen, recognizing causal links, and inferring likely consequences are essential for true language understanding, going far beyond mere pattern matching or syntactic parsing. Recent years have witnessed growing interest within the NLP community directed toward imbuing machines with commonsense reasoning capabilities. From knowledge graph construction and completion (e.g., ConceptNet, ATOMIC) to neural approaches like pre-trained language models (e.g., BERT, GPT-3), researchers have explored diverse strategies to equip systems with background knowledge and reasoning mechanisms. However, progress is often hampered by a fundamental bottleneck: the scarcity of robust and targeted evaluation frameworks. Existing benchmarks often focus on explicit knowledge facts, reasoning over structured data, or simplified scenarios, falling short of capturing the complexity and subtlety of commonsense inference required for genuine story understanding. Consider the simple task of following a narrative. Humans not only track the sequence of events but also anticipate likely outcomes, fill in missing information, and understand the motivations driving the characters’ actions. This process relies heavily on unstated, commonsense understandings about how the world works. Current evaluation methods frequently fail to adequately assess whether a system has *learned* these underlying principles, or is merely exploiting superficial statistical correlations present in training data. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel framework for evaluating a system's capacity to understand commonsense stories: the *Story Cloze Test*. This test presents a system with a four-sentence story and asks it to select the most plausible fifth sentence from a set of candidate endings. Success hinges not on recalling specific facts, but on demonstrating an understanding of causal and temporal relationships, event plausibility, and character motivations – all crucial components of commonsense reasoning. To facilitate this evaluation, we have created *ROCStories*, a new corpus of 50,000 five-sentence commonsense stories. This corpus is distinct in two key aspects. First, ROCStories is intentionally designed to emphasize rich causal and temporal commonsense relations between everyday events, offering a more focused challenge than existing narrative datasets. Second, the stories are written as coherent and grammatically correct narratives reflecting typical everyday life scenarios, thereby also offering a valuable resource for story generation tasks. Through extensive experimentation with a variety of baseline and state-of-the-art models, we demonstrate that achieving strong performance on the Story Cloze Test is surprisingly difficult, even for models exhibiting impressive performance on other language understanding benchmarks. Our results suggest that current approaches, relying primarily on shallow language understanding techniques, struggle to capture the deeper commonsense reasoning required for robust story comprehension. We provide a detailed analysis of these shortcomings and discuss the implications for future research in script and story learning, suggesting avenues toward more robust and genuinely understanding language models.

Dialogue is fundamentally a cooperative endeavor. From Grice’s maxims to more formal dialogue game theories, a presupposition underlying much of natural language processing and computational linguistics research is that participants generally *intend* to facilitate mutual understanding. However, real-world dialogue is frequently riddled with instances of non-cooperation, ranging from subtle conversational roadblocks to overt refusals to engage. Understanding, and crucially, *measuring* non-cooperation is therefore critical for building robust and nuanced dialogue systems, analyzing human interactions, and even diagnosing communication breakdowns in social settings. Existing approaches to modelling non-cooperation fall broadly into two categories. The first focuses on task-related non-cooperation, typically observed in goal-oriented dialogues where participants might deliberately withhold information or provide misleading answers to achieve a preferred outcome. This work, while valuable, is limited in scope, as it fails to capture non-cooperative behaviours driven by factors beyond immediate task success – such as politeness strategies, power dynamics, or deliberate obfuscation. The second existing approach attempts to model non-cooperation through explicitly defined rules governing ‘bad’ conversational behavior. This often involves defining specific non-cooperative acts, like interrupting, or changing the subject, and then identifying their occurrence in a dialogue. However, this requires a substantial degree of manual specification and struggles to account for the subtle, context-dependent nature of non-cooperation. Furthermore, defining what constitutes “non-cooperative” behavior can be inherently subjective and reliant on pre-defined assumptions about the interaction. This paper proposes a novel approach that sidesteps these limitations by framing non-cooperation not as a set of positive rules describing *what not to do*, but as a *deviation from norms* of cooperative behaviour. We argue that linguistic non-cooperation can be quantified by assessing the extent to which a dialogue participant violates conventions governing the proper introduction and discharging of conversational obligations, as defined within a formal dialogue game framework. Instead of pre-defining non-cooperative acts, we begin with a model of *normal* dialogue – a set of rules describing how a cooperative conversation should unfold – and then measure the degree to which actual utterances comply with those rules. This framework offers significant advantages: the rules underlying expected cooperative behavior can, in principle, be learned automatically from large corpora of cooperative dialogues, reducing reliance on hand-crafted features and subjective annotations. This also facilitates a more nuanced understanding of non-cooperation, allowing us to quantify it on a continuous scale rather than simply labeling utterances as cooperative or non-cooperative. We operationalize this approach with a formal dialogue game, and demonstrate its efficacy on a corpus of political interviews – a domain where non-cooperation is often strategically employed. Our evaluation demonstrates that our model can accurately predict the degree of cooperation exhibited by one of the dialogue roles (the interviewer) and, importantly, can discern *relative* levels of cooperation between participants, identifying which interlocutor is exhibiting more or less cooperative behaviour at each turn. This ability to assess relative cooperation is critical for understanding power dynamics and rhetorical strategies employed in these interactions. The implications of this work extend beyond simple analysis; a robust measure of dialogue cooperation has potential applications in a wide range of areas, from improving the design of human-computer interfaces to creating more engaging and realistic virtual agents and tutoring systems.

Automated Essay Scoring (AES) has emerged as a critical component in large-scale educational assessments, offering a scalable and cost-effective alternative to traditional human grading. The potential benefits are substantial, ranging from providing immediate feedback to students, facilitating formative assessment, and freeing up educators' time for more personalized instruction. However, a longstanding challenge in AES lies in the performance degradation when a model trained on essays from one prompt is applied to essays responding to a different, unseen prompt. This phenomenon, indicative of domain shift, significantly limits the practical applicability of many AES systems. The core issue stems from the inherent variability in essay content and expression prompted by different assignments. Even seemingly similar prompts can elicit divergent writing styles, topical focuses, and argumentation strategies. Consequently, models trained to identify the hallmarks of quality within a specific prompt's context often struggle when confronted with a new prompt exhibiting distinct characteristics. The idealized solution – retraining the AES model with a significant corpus of human-scored essays for *each* new prompt – is frequently impractical. Securing reliable and representative essay collections, coupled with the expensive and time-consuming process of expert scoring, presents a major bottleneck to widespread AES deployment. This paper addresses the problem of prompt-based domain shift in AES through the lens of domain adaptation. Domain adaptation techniques aim to bridge the gap between a source domain (the prompt on which the model is initially trained) and a target domain (the new, unseen prompt) without requiring extensive labeled data in the target domain. Existing approaches to domain adaptation in AES have explored various methods, including feature transformations, adversarial training, and transfer learning using pre-trained language models. However, many of these techniques can be computationally expensive, require careful hyperparameter tuning, or rely on complex model architectures that reduce interpretability. Furthermore, they often treat the domain adaptation problem as a black box, rather than explicitly modeling the relationships between prompts and essay qualities. We propose a novel and efficient domain adaptation technique for AES grounded in Bayesian linear ridge regression. This approach leverages the inherent structure in model parameters learned across different prompts, recognizing that the relationship between essay features and scores is often correlated across tasks. Specifically, we model the target domain's prediction function as a linear combination of the source domain's parameters, weighted by correlations derived from prompt similarity. This correlated linear regression approach allows for a flexible and interpretable transfer of knowledge, minimizing the need for substantial target domain data while effectively adapting the AES model to the nuances of the new prompt. Our method provides several key advantages. First, it’s computationally lightweight, suitable for real-time adaptation. Second, the Bayesian framework naturally provides uncertainty estimates, indicating the reliability of predictions on the target domain. Third, by explicitly modeling parameter correlations, the approach provides insights into *how* knowledge is transferred between prompts. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using the publicly available Automated Student Assessment Prize (ASAP) dataset, showcasing competitive performance against established domain adaptation baselines. This work contributes a practical and theoretically sound solution to a central challenge in automated essay scoring, paving the way for more robust and generalizable AES systems.

Named Entity Recognition (NER) forms a foundational component in numerous Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications, including information extraction, question answering, and machine translation. Modern, state-of-the-art NER systems predominantly leverage statistical machine learning models – particularly deep learning architectures – that excel at generalizing to unseen entities based on learned lexical and contextual patterns. These models demonstrate a remarkable capacity to identify entities not explicitly encountered during training, a crucial ability for real-world deployment where exhaustive enumeration of entities is impractical. However, despite their advances, these systems remain susceptible to assigning incorrect entity types, particularly in scenarios involving ambiguity or limited training data. A model might correctly *identify* a span of text as an entity, but misclassify it as, for instance, a ‘PERSON’ when it should be an ‘ORGANIZATION,’ ultimately hindering downstream task performance. A significant factor contributing to these errors lies in the reliance solely on textual features. While contextual information is potent, it often lacks the explicit knowledge needed to disambiguate entities and accurately determine their type. Consider the entity “Apple”; without broader context, it’s ambiguous whether it refers to the technology company or the fruit. This is where external knowledge sources become invaluable. This paper explores the integration of Wikipedia, a vast and readily available open knowledge base, to enhance the accuracy of multilingual NER systems. We hypothesize that by grounding entity recognition in a structured knowledge representation like Wikipedia, we can significantly improve type disambiguation and generalization performance. Our central contribution is the construction of comprehensive, high-accuracy, and high-coverage multilingual Wikipedia entity type mappings. These mappings, which link Wikipedia entities to their corresponding types, are built utilizing a weakly supervised approach that minimizes the need for extensive manual annotation. Crucially, the methodology is designed for scalability and language independence, enabling the effortless extension of the mappings to new languages without requiring language-specific expertise or costly human intervention. Existing methods for incorporating knowledge bases into NER often rely on resource-intensive, manually curated datasets or language-specific rule sets. In contrast, our approach leverages the inherent structure of Wikipedia and a novel training paradigm to bootstrap high-quality mappings automatically. We then investigate several strategies for effectively utilizing these mappings to refine NER predictions, ranging from feature augmentation to constrained decoding. We evaluate our approach extensively across NER systems trained and tested on six diverse languages. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed techniques in improving NER accuracy, particularly in recognizing unseen entities – a critical aspect for adapting models to new domains or operating with limited labelled training data. Specifically, we observe substantial performance gains, with F1 score improvements of up to 18.3% in challenging scenarios. This work represents a significant step towards building more robust, accurate, and adaptable multilingual NER systems that can leverage the wealth of information contained in open knowledge bases like Wikipedia. --- Does this introduction meet the requirements? Automatic keyphrase generation (KPG) aims to automatically identify and extract or generate a set of representative phrases that summarize the main topics of a given document. It serves as a crucial component in numerous natural language processing (NLP) applications, including information retrieval, document summarization, and content recommendation. Traditionally, KPG has been approached through either extractive or generative paradigms. Extractive methods, stemming from early work in statistical keyphrase extraction (Turney, 2000; Witten et al., 2008), identify existing phrases within the document that best represent its content. While computationally efficient, these methods are limited by the vocabulary present in the source text and struggle to capture abstract concepts or synthesize novel phrases. Generative approaches, leveraging the advancements in sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models (Sutskever et al., 2014; Cho et al., 2014), have gained prominence due to their ability to generate keyphrases not explicitly present in the original document. Initial generative KPG models (Hashim et al., 2016; Mesnil et al., 2015) exhibited promising results, but often suffered from issues like repetition, lack of diversity, and inadequate coverage of document content. Subsequent works attempted to address these limitations by incorporating attention mechanisms (Bahdanau et al., 2015), copy mechanisms (Gu et al., 2018), and reinforcement learning techniques (Li et al., 2018). However, a recurring challenge in generative KPG, largely overlooked by existing methods, is the inherent correlation *between* generated keyphrases. Consider a document discussing "artificial intelligence in healthcare." A strong KPG system should ideally generate phrases like “machine learning applications”, “medical diagnosis”, or “patient data analysis” as representative keyphrases. These concepts are not independent; they are interlinked and contribute to a cohesive understanding of the document's theme. Existing models, primarily focusing on generating phrases one at a time, often fail to capture these relationships, leading to redundant keyphrases (e.g., "artificial intelligence" and "AI") or incomplete coverage of core topics, as phrases may address aspects of the same topic without reflecting the full breadth of the concept. The problem of neglecting keyphrase correlation manifests in two primary ways: *duplication* – generating phrases that convey similar information, diminishing the overall informativeness of the keyphrase set – and *coverage issues* – failing to capture all significant thematic elements of the document due to the absence of correlated phrases. To address these limitations, we introduce CorrRNN, a novel sequence-to-sequence architecture specifically designed for keyphrase generation with correlation constraints. CorrRNN incorporates two key mechanisms: a coverage vector that dynamically tracks which parts of the source document have been adequately summarized by previously generated phrases, thereby promoting broader content coverage; and a mechanism for attending to preceding generated phrases, discouraging the repetition of similar concepts and fostering coherence within the generated keyphrase set. Our experiments on widely-used benchmark datasets demonstrate that CorrRNN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art KPG models in terms of both keyphrase accuracy and diversity, establishing the importance of explicitly modelling inter-keyphrase correlations.

Graphical models provide a powerful framework for representing and reasoning about complex dependencies between variables. They find broad application across diverse fields, including natural language processing, computer vision, and bioinformatics. However, exact inference in these models is often intractable, necessitating the use of approximation techniques. Among these, Belief Propagation (BP) and its variants remain popular choices due to their relative simplicity and potential for efficient computation. Yet, standard BP often suffers from inaccuracies when applied to models with cycles (loopy belief propagation) or with non-trivial factor structures. Expectation Propagation (EP) offers an improvement over standard BP by adopting a more principled approach to approximate inference. Rather than iteratively passing messages without regard for global consistency, EP focuses on sequentially approximating each factor in the model by a member of a tractable family, ensuring that the resulting approximate posterior matches key moments of the true posterior. This localized updating strategy, coupled with the flexibility to choose appropriate approximating families, allows EP to often outperform standard BP. Despite these advantages, the computational cost of EP can still be significant, particularly when dealing with complex models and large datasets. Maintaining tractability of the approximate messages often requires careful design of the approximating family, and the iterative message passing process can be slow to converge. A central challenge in applying EP—and indeed, many approximate inference algorithms—is striking a balance between accuracy and computational efficiency. More complex approximating families generally lead to more accurate approximations but also to increased computational cost. Conversely, simpler approximations are faster to compute but may sacrifice accuracy. This paper introduces Penalized Expectation Propagation (PEP), a novel extension of EP designed to address this trade-off. PEP incorporates a structured sparsity penalty into the EP update rules, explicitly encouraging the selection of simpler, more parsimonious approximate messages. By favoring simplicity, PEP aims to accelerate convergence and reduce the computational burden without significant degradation in accuracy. We focus our investigation on graphical models over *strings*, a common representation in many NLP tasks such as phonological inference, speech recognition, and machine translation. Reasoning about strings often requires modeling complex dependencies between sequential elements. While traditional approaches to string modeling, like Hidden Markov Models (HMMs), offer tractability, they often suffer from limitations in expressiveness. More powerful models, like variable-order n-gram models, capture richer dependencies but pose significant computational challenges for inference. Our contribution is a specific instantiation of PEP tailored for these string-valued graphical models. We adaptively approximate finite-state distributions using variable-order n-gram models, guided by the sparsity penalty to control model complexity. This allows us to reap the benefits of higher-order dependencies where they are most informative, while avoiding the computational expense of excessively complex models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PEP on challenging phonological inference problems, showcasing substantial speedups over previous state-of-the-art algorithms without a noticeable reduction in accuracy. Through empirical evaluation, we demonstrate that PEP offers a compelling solution for approximate inference in string-valued graphical models, providing a practical balance between computational efficiency and accuracy.

Relation extraction (RE) – the task of identifying semantic relationships between entities in text – is a core component of many natural language processing applications, including knowledge base construction, question answering, and information retrieval. Traditionally, RE systems relied on meticulously hand-annotated datasets, a process both expensive and time-consuming, hindering the scalability of these systems to diverse domains and relationships. Distant supervision (DS), introduced by Mintz et al. (2009), offered a compelling alternative by automatically generating training instances based on existing knowledge bases. The underlying assumption is that if two entities in a sentence are related in a knowledge base, the sentence likely expresses that relation. This approach dramatically reduces the need for manual annotation, enabling the creation of large-scale RE training datasets with minimal human effort. However, the inherent heuristic nature of DS introduces significant noise. The “distant supervision assumption” is frequently violated—a sentence may mention two entities related in a knowledge base without actually *expressing* that relation. For example, a sentence mentioning "Barack Obama" and "United States" might appear in a context discussing his birth location, rather than his presidency. Despite various filtering techniques and noise reduction strategies proposed in prior work, DS-generated datasets remain substantially noisier than manually curated ones. This noise fundamentally impacts model performance, limiting the effectiveness of even sophisticated learning algorithms. Existing approaches to address this noise fall into several categories. Some focus on instance selection (Hoffmann et al., 2016; Yao et al., 2019), attempting to identify and discard noisy instances. Others explore multi-instance learning (Riedel et al., 2013), treating each sentence as a bag of instances and aiming to learn from the presence of at least one correct instance. Graph-based methods (Lin et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018) leverage the graph structure of the knowledge base to propagate information and refine relation labels. More recently, attention mechanisms (Liu et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2020) have been employed to selectively focus on the most relevant parts of sentences to mitigate the influence of irrelevant noise. While these methods offer improvements, they often rely on complex models or require additional resources, and a robust, generalizable solution to the DS noise problem remains an open challenge. In this paper, we present a novel approach to enhance distantly supervised relation extraction by explicitly modeling and mitigating noise using a dynamic transition matrix. We posit that the process of noisy label generation can be viewed as a transition process between true and false relation labels, and the transition matrix governs this process. Crucially, our method *learns* this transition matrix directly from the data, without requiring any explicit supervision regarding which instances are noisy or clean. We propose a curriculum learning scheme that gradually refines the transition matrix, starting from a uniform initialization and iteratively adjusting it based on the model’s performance on progressively more challenging examples. This dynamic learning process allows the model to adapt to the specific characteristics of the noise present in the training data. We conduct extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets for relation extraction, evaluating our method under a wide range of extraction scenarios. Our results demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving significant improvements in precision, recall, and F1-score. ## Introduction Readability – the ease with which a reader can comprehend a text – is a cornerstone of effective communication. Ensuring text is appropriately tailored to its intended audience is paramount across a wide spectrum of applications, from educational materials and public health information to news reporting and legal documents. While significant progress has been made in computational readability assessment for languages like English, research on languages beyond the commonly studied Indo-European family remains relatively sparse. This gap is particularly pronounced for morphologically rich languages like Bangla, spoken by over 265 million people worldwide, making it the seventh most spoken language globally. Bangla presents unique challenges to automated readability assessment. Its complex morphology, flexible word order, and a rich set of compound verbs and postpositions contribute to sentence structures that can differ significantly from languages where readability models are well-established. Existing, limited work in Bangla readability often focuses on simple, feature-based approaches employing character and word counts, largely mirroring early English readability formulas like the Flesch Reading Ease. However, these "classic" features often fall short of capturing the nuances that truly determine how a reader perceives difficulty in a language as complex as Bangla. Moreover, a critical yet frequently overlooked aspect of readability is the *reader* themselves. Readability is not an intrinsic property of a text, but rather a relationship between the text and the reader’s linguistic background, cognitive abilities, prior knowledge, and educational level. A text considered “easy” for a native speaker with a strong educational background may pose significant challenges to a reader with limited formal education or a different linguistic background. This is particularly relevant in the context of Bangla, where educational attainment and exposure to standardized written language varies substantially across different socio-economic groups and regional dialects. This paper addresses these limitations by presenting a comprehensive computational investigation into Bangla text readability, focusing on the interplay between *target reader characteristics* and *textual features*. We move beyond traditional, solely text-based readability measures by introducing a novel, reader-annotated dataset comprising 135 Bangla documents assessed by 50 readers representing two distinct background groups – university students and individuals with secondary-level education. This allows us to directly examine how perceptions of text difficulty differ based on reader background. We identify and analyze 20 features potentially influencing Bangla readability, categorized as “classic” (e.g., average sentence length, syllable count) and “non-classic” (e.g., the frequency of complex verb forms, number of conjunct consonants, and use of specific grammatical constructions). Through preliminary correlation analysis, we demonstrate that the influence of these features on perceived difficulty varies significantly between the two reader groups. We then leverage Support Vector Machines (SVM) and Support Vector Regression (SVR) to model reading difficulty, developing separate models tailored to each reader background and evaluating the impacts of various feature combinations. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive computational study specifically designed to address the influence of reader background on Bangla text readability, employing a substantial reader-annotated dataset and a rigorous feature-based analysis. Our findings offer valuable insights into the factors that govern comprehension in Bangla and pave the way for the development of more effective and user-centric readability assessment tools for this important language.

Understanding the relationships between mentions of entities across a collection of documents is a fundamental task in natural language processing, with broad applications in information retrieval, question answering, and knowledge base construction. Two core problems address this challenge: cross-document co-reference resolution (CCR) and named-entity linking (NEL). CCR aims to identify all mentions within a corpus that refer to the same real-world entity, forming equivalence classes of co-referring mentions. NEL, on the other hand, focuses on disambiguating these mentions by linking them to their corresponding entries in a pre-defined knowledge base (KB), such as Wikidata or DBpedia, or determining that a mention does not have a representation in the KB—a "nil" entity. Historically, CCR and NEL have been largely treated as independent tasks, each with its own dedicated methodologies and datasets. Traditional CCR approaches often operate by defining feature-based models or, more recently, leveraging deep learning architectures to assess the similarity between mention pairs, considering factors like string overlap, contextual similarity, and entity type compatibility. Similarly, NEL predominantly employs methods that rank candidate entities from a KB based on mention context, entity prior probabilities, and similarity measures. However, this separation overlooks a crucial and readily exploitable interdependency. The accurate resolution of co-references can significantly aid NEL. Knowing that multiple mentions across documents refer to the same entity provides additional contextual information, improving the likelihood of correctly identifying the corresponding KB entry. Conversely, successful NEL can powerfully enhance CCR. Linking mentions to their KB counterparts provides valuable ‘distant supervision’ – essentially, ground truth co-reference links derived from the structure of the knowledge base. If two mentions, appearing in different documents, both link to the same KB entity, it provides strong evidence that they are co-referent, even if textual similarity is low. This paper introduces C3EL (Cross-document Co-reference and Entity Linking), an unsupervised framework designed to capitalize on this synergy by jointly modeling CCR and NEL. C3EL is not merely a pipeline of sequential steps; instead, it’s an iterative algorithm where the outputs of NEL inform CCR, and *vice versa*. We incorporate global context gleaned from the CCR stage to enrich the feature space used for NEL, thereby improving its performance. Simultaneously, we utilize the disambiguated entities discovered by NEL to provide informative KB features to the CCR stage, bolstering its ability to identify co-referring mentions. Specifically, by leveraging information about already linked mentions, we can propagate evidence of co-reference based on KB-derived relationships. Our iterative approach strategically focuses on resolving the highest-confidence, yet still unresolved, mentions in each iteration, ensuring efficient convergence. This contrasts with other joint models that may struggle with scalability or require extensive training data. To demonstrate the effectiveness of C3EL, we conduct experiments on two diverse corpora—a news-centric dataset and a more challenging web-centric dataset—and compare our results with established state-of-the-art baselines for both CCR and NEL. Our findings consistently show that the joint modeling approach offered by C3EL yields significant performance gains over independent, and even previously proposed joint, methods, highlighting the benefits of tightly integrating these two crucial NLP tasks.

Multi-task learning (MTL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm in natural language processing, offering a compelling strategy for improving model performance and generalization capabilities – particularly when training data is limited for individual tasks. The core principle of MTL relies on the idea that learning multiple related tasks concurrently can facilitate knowledge transfer, leveraging shared representations to boost the performance of each task involved. A common implementation of MTL in neural networks involves sharing parameters, either through hard parameter sharing (where layers are directly linked across tasks) or soft parameter sharing (where models have their own parameters but are regularized to be similar). Recent advances have demonstrated the effectiveness of MTL across a diverse range of NLP applications including sentiment analysis, topic classification, and natural language inference. However, the success of MTL is predicated on the assumption that tasks are sufficiently related and that the shared knowledge is beneficial. In practice, simply forcing the sharing of features does not always lead to improvements; it can, in fact, introduce *negative transfer*, where the performance on one or more tasks is degraded due to interference from others. Existing multi-task learning architectures often lack a sophisticated mechanism for determining *what* knowledge should be shared, and *when* or *with whom* it should be shared. Essentially, they treat all shared features as equally valuable, overlooking the fundamental possibility that features beneficial to one task may be detrimental to another. This issue of interference is particularly prominent in text classification scenarios where tasks often have varying degrees of semantic and stylistic complexities. For instance, attempting to share low-level linguistic features between sentiment analysis and topic categorization might introduce noise, as the relevant feature spaces for distinguishing positive/negative sentiment are conceptually different from those used to identify document themes. Standard shared-layer approaches can lead to a “contamination” of feature spaces, where task-specific representations are diluted or distorted by irrelevant information propagated from other tasks. A model ends up learning not only what is useful for its assigned task but also potentially absorbing distracting signals from others, ultimately hindering its predictive capacity. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel multi-task convolutional neural network architecture incorporating a “Leaky Unit”. This unit functions as a dynamic gate, employing a memory and forgetting mechanism to selectively filter feature flows between tasks. Unlike traditional approaches that passively share features, our Leaky Unit learns to determine the relevance of each feature for each specific task, effectively controlling the amount of information transferred. By enabling a task to “forget” irrelevant features from other tasks, we mitigate the problem of negative transfer and promote more focused and effective learning. We rigorously evaluate our approach on five diverse text classification datasets, demonstrating significant performance gains compared to both single-task baselines and state-of-the-art MTL methods. Our results highlight the importance of a selective feature-sharing mechanism in MTL for text classification, showing that learning *what* to share is as critical as *how* to share. This paper contributes a practical and effective solution for enhancing knowledge transfer in MTL systems, leading to more robust and accurate text classification models.

Statistical machine translation (SMT) has long leveraged the power of synchronous context-free grammars (SCFGs) to model non-local dependencies between source and target languages, offering a principled framework for capturing syntactic agreement and reordering phenomena crucial for high-quality translation. However, the theoretical strengths of SCFGs are often tempered by the computational challenges associated with decoding. A fundamental tenet in the field has been that efficient, polynomial-time decoding with SCFGs – specifically, cubic time complexity – necessitates a transformation into a specific normal form. Traditionally, this has meant converting SCFGs into Chomsky Normal Form (CNF) via the synchronous binarization process introduced by Zhang et al. (2006). While mathematically sound, synchronous binarization introduces a significant practical bottleneck. The process of expanding non-binary rules in an SCFG fundamentally *inflates* the grammar size. This expansion dramatically increases the constant factors involved in decoding algorithms like the Earley algorithm or variants optimized for SMT, leading to considerably slower practical performance. DeNero et al. (2009) elegantly addressed this issue by proposing Lexical Normal Form (LNF), a stricter but more compact normal form that, under certain conditions, also enables cubic-time decoding. Their work represented a substantial step toward bridging the gap between theoretical efficiency and practical speed in SCFG-based SMT. However, the conditions under which LNF guarantees cubic-time decoding have remained largely implicit, hindering a complete understanding of its capabilities and limitations. Furthermore, the potential for extending the class of grammars beyond LNF, while maintaining this critical cubic-time property, has remained largely unexplored. In this paper, we rigorously examine these implicit assumptions regarding LNF’s efficiency, making them explicit and formulating a broader grammar class we term “scope-3.” We demonstrate that grammars in the scope-3 class inherit the properties that ensure cubic-time decoding, effectively expanding the space of allowable grammars beyond LNF without sacrificing computational efficiency. Critically, we show how to identify and prune rules that fall *outside* of the scope-3 class from grammars typically extracted using the GHKM method (Galley et al., 2004), a commonly used technique for deriving SCFGs from parallel corpora. Our experimental results demonstrate that this simple pruning strategy, operating on GHKM-extracted grammars to adhere to the scope-3 constraints, consistently yields superior translation performance compared to traditional synchronous binarization. By avoiding the grammar inflation inherent in binarization and leveraging a broader, yet provably efficient, grammar class, our approach represents a significant advance in practical SCFG decoding for SMT.
